etymology: From Latin absens, present participle of abesse, to be away, from ab (from) and esse (to be). Webster 1828: not present; away. Paul uses the word for the believer’s death, and in doing so denies the soul any interval of sleep or unconsciousness.
biblical_def: Paul’s statement about dying is short and it settles a great deal: We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). Two propositions are joined by nothing but a comma, and the joining is the doctrine — absence from the body is presence with the Lord, with no third condition between them. The chapter has already used the figure of a tent taken down and a house not made with hands, and Philippians 1:23 says the same thing from the other side: to depart and to be with Christ is far better. The word also does ordinary apostolic work. Paul rules on a case in Corinth without being there: I verily, as absent in body, but present in spirit, have judged already (1 Corinthians 5:3) — and the judgment is real church discipline, not sentiment. To the Philippians he ties his absence to their steadfastness: that whether I come and see you, or else be absent, I may hear of your affairs, that ye stand fast in one spirit (Philippians 1:27). A church is what it is when the apostle is not watching.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ABSENT as not present; not in company; at such a distance as to prevent communication; and figuratively, heedless, inattentive to what is passing.
webster_full: ABSENT, a. — Not present; not in company; at such a distance as to prevent communication.
Heedless; inattentive to persons present, or to subjects of conversation.
ABSENT, v.t. — To depart to such a distance as to prevent intercourse; to retire or withdraw.
ABSENCE, n. — A state of being at a distance in place; want; destitution.
Latin absens, from ab, from, and sum, esse, to be.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 5:8
We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord.
1 Corinthians 5:3
For I verily, as absent in body, but present in spirit, have judged already, as though I were present, concerning him that hath so done this deed,
Philippians 1:27

Only let your conversation be as it becometh the gospel of Christ: that whether I come and see you, or else be absent, I may hear of your affairs, that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel;
Colossians 2:5
For though I be absent in the flesh, yet am I with you in the spirit, joying and beholding your order, and the stedfastness of your faith in Christ.
corruption_summary: 2 Corinthians 5:8 leaves no room for soul sleep, purgatory, or annihilation at death: the believer who is absent from the body is at that moment present with the Lord.
corruption_paragraphs: Three errors are excluded by this one verse. Soul sleep — the teaching that the soul is unconscious between death and resurrection, held by the Seventh-day Adventists and the Jehovah’s Witnesses — cannot survive a text in which absence from the body is presence with Christ; an unconscious presence is not what Paul means by far better (Philippians 1:23), nor what our Lord promised the thief for that same day (Luke 23:43). Purgatory is excluded by the same immediacy: if the believer is with the Lord upon dying, there is no penal interval to be shortened by masses or indulgences, and the doctrine that supplies one denies the sufficiency of Christ’s satisfaction. Annihilationism is excluded because the one who is absent from the body still exists to be present with someone. The 1689 Confession states the settled position: the souls of the righteous are received into the highest heavens, and the souls of the wicked cast into hell, and besides these two places Scripture acknowledges none.

A second point belongs here, because the intermediate state is often preached as though it were the whole hope. It is not. Paul’s longing in 2 Corinthians 5 is not to be a disembodied spirit but to be clothed upon — he says explicitly that he does not wish to be found naked. Being with Christ at death is far better; the resurrection of the body is better still, and it is the Christian hope properly so called. Funeral preaching that stops at the soul in heaven has stopped one article short of the creed, which confesses the resurrection of the body and the life everlasting.
roots_summary: Greek ekdemeo (G1553), to be away from home, to be absent; endemeo (G1736), to be at home, to be present; apeimi (G548), to be away.
roots_lines: Greek ekdemeo (G1553) — to be out of one’s home country, to be absent; absent from the body (2 Corinthians 5:8).
Greek endemeo (G1736) — to be at home, to be present; the deliberate counterpart in the same verse.
Greek apeimi (G548) — to be away; used of Paul’s bodily absence from Corinth and Colosse (1 Corinthians 5:3; Colossians 2:5).
Greek analuo (G360) — to loose anchor, to depart; to depart, and to be with Christ (Philippians 1:23).
Greek skenos (G4636) — a tent or tabernacle, Paul’s figure for the body in 2 Corinthians 5:1.
usage: Absent from the body, and... present with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8) — two propositions joined by a comma, with no third state between them.
Absent in body, but present in spirit, have judged already (1 Corinthians 5:3) — real church discipline exercised at a distance.
Whether I come and see you, or else be absent... ye stand fast (Philippians 1:27) — a church is what it is unwatched.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon ealmaest, from eall (all) and maest (most): very nearly, all but. Webster 1828: nearly; well nigh; for the greatest part. In Scripture it is the saddest adverb in the book, and also the mark of a saint’s narrow escape.
biblical_def: Agrippa’s reply to Paul is the most famous almost in Scripture, and its tone is disputed — irony or genuine stirring — but its outcome is not: Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian (Acts 26:28). The king heard the resurrection argued by a chained man, felt the force of it, and adjourned. Paul’s answer in the next verse wishes him and all his hearers altogether such as he was, except the bonds. Against this stands the word used by a saint describing how nearly he fell: But as for me, my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped (Psalm 73:2). Asaph had envied the prosperity of the wicked until he went into the sanctuary and understood their end; the almost here is the measure of a preserving grace, not of a lost opportunity. The psalmist elsewhere reports the same narrowness under persecution: They had almost consumed me upon earth; but I forsook not thy precepts (Psalm 119:87). The difference between Agrippa and Asaph is not the nearness of the margin but who was holding them.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ALMOST as nearly; well nigh; all but; for the greatest part — that is, wanting only a little of the whole.
webster_full: ALMOST, adv. — Nearly; well nigh; for the greatest part.
All but; wanting little of.
Used to qualify a statement which is very nearly, but not entirely, true.
From all and most; Anglo-Saxon ealmaest.
Compare the older English wellnigh, of the same force.
scriptures: Acts 26:28
Then Agrippa said unto Paul, Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian.
Psalm 73:2
But as for me, my feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped.
Psalm 119:87
They had almost consumed me upon earth; but I forsook not thy precepts.
Acts 26:29
And Paul said, I would to God, that not only thou, but also all that hear me this day, were both almost, and altogether such as I am, except these bonds.
corruption_summary: An almost-Christian is not a partial Christian, and the modern practice of counting decisions rather than looking for fruit has produced a great many people who believe themselves inside on the strength of a moment of feeling.
corruption_paragraphs: The Puritans wrote whole treatises on this word — Matthew Mead’s The Almost Christian Discovered is the best known — because they understood that the most dangerous spiritual condition is not open unbelief but a near approach that stops short. An almost-Christian may have doctrinal knowledge, moral reformation, religious affections, and public reputation, and still be unregenerate, because none of those things is the new birth. The modern practice of counting responses to an appeal and treating the response itself as the moment of salvation has multiplied this condition and then insulated it, since the convert is taught to settle every later doubt by appealing to the day he decided. Scripture directs the anxious elsewhere: examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith (2 Corinthians 13:5), and the marks it gives are fruit, love of the brethren, and perseverance — not the recollection of a decision.

Psalm 73 supplies the corrective on the other side, and it is needed, because the doctrine above can be preached into despair. Asaph’s feet were almost gone. He confesses envy of the wicked, bitterness of heart, and by his own account behaved as a beast before God (Psalm 73:22). He was not almost a believer; he was a believer almost fallen — and the psalm ends with God holding him by his right hand and guiding him with His counsel. The Reformed doctrine of perseverance is not the claim that the saints never stagger; it is the claim that God keeps those He has given to His Son. The distance between Agrippa and Asaph is not measured in the narrowness of the margin but in whose hand was on them.
roots_summary: Greek oligos (G3641), little, in the phrase en oligo, in a little, almost; schedon (G4975), nearly; Hebrew meat (H4592), a little, a trifle.
roots_lines: Greek en oligo — literally in a little; Agrippa’s phrase, rendered almost in the Authorized Version (Acts 26:28).
Greek schedon (G4975) — nearly, almost; used of the whole city gathered in Acts 13:44.
Hebrew meat (H4592) — a little, a small amount; my feet were almost gone (Psalm 73:2).
Hebrew kimat (H3644 with H4592) — well nigh, very nearly; the doubled expression of Psalm 73:2.
Greek peitho (G3982) — to persuade; the verb Agrippa uses and Paul answers (Acts 26:28-29).
usage: Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian (Acts 26:28) — the king felt the force of it and adjourned.
My feet were almost gone; my steps had well nigh slipped (Psalm 73:2) — a believer almost fallen, not an almost-believer.
Both almost, and altogether such as I am, except these bonds (Acts 26:29) — Paul refuses to leave the word where Agrippa left it.

etymology: From Anglo-Saxon sped, success, prosperity, good fortune — the sense of swiftness is later. Webster 1828: success; prosperity in an undertaking; hence the old greeting God speed, a wish for God’s prosperity upon a man’s way.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version preserves the older meaning, in which speed is success rather than swiftness. Abraham’s servant, sent to find a wife for Isaac, prays for it by name: O LORD God of my master Abraham, I pray thee, send me good speed this day, and shew kindness unto my master Abraham (Genesis 24:12). He is asking for prosperity in the errand, and the chapter is one of the clearest narratives of ordinary providence in Scripture — the answer arrives before he has finished speaking. The word’s most weighty use is a prohibition. John forbids the church to pronounce that blessing over a false teacher: If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house, neither bid him God speed (2 John 1:10), and he gives the reason in the next breath: he that biddeth him God speed is partaker of his evil deeds (2 John 1:11). To wish a man success is to take a share in what he is doing. The apostle of love writes this, and it is not an inconsistency; love for the flock requires that its enemies not be sped on their way with a blessing.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SPEED as success; prosperity in an undertaking; favorable issue; and secondarily swiftness, quickness, celerity. The phrase God speed is a wish for prosperity upon a man’s undertaking.
webster_full: SPEED, n. — Success; prosperity in an undertaking; favorable issue; as, to bid one good speed.
Swiftness; quickness; celerity; haste; dispatch.
SPEED, v.i. — To make haste; to move with celerity; also, to have success; to prosper.
SPEED, v.t. — To dispatch; to send away in haste; to hasten; also, to prosper; to cause to succeed.
Anglo-Saxon sped, success, from spedan, to prosper — the sense of swiftness is secondary and later.
scriptures: Genesis 24:12
And he said, O LORD God of my master Abraham, I pray thee, send me good speed this day, and shew kindness unto my master Abraham.
2 John 1:10
If there come any unto you, and bring not this doctrine, receive him not into your house, neither bid him God speed:
2 John 1:11
For he that biddeth him God speed is partaker of his evil deeds.
Genesis 24:27
And he said, Blessed be the LORD God of my master Abraham, who hath not left destitute my master of his mercy and his truth: I being in the way, the LORD led me to the house of my master's brethren.
corruption_summary: 2 John 1:10-11 forbids extending the church’s blessing to a teacher who denies the doctrine of Christ, and the modern reflex to call every such refusal unloving has the apostle of love against it.
corruption_paragraphs: The instruction is precise and it is limited. John is not addressing personal rudeness toward unbelievers, nor secondary disagreements among brethren; the doctrine of Christ in view is the incarnation itself, denied by the deceivers of verse 7 who confess not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh. Against that specific denial the church is told to withhold hospitality and greeting, on the stated ground that a blessing makes the blesser a partaker. This cuts directly against the ecumenical instinct that treats joint platforms and public warmth as costless expressions of charity. They are not costless; John says they transfer a share in the deeds. The 1689 Confession’s chapter on the church assumes exactly this discipline, and the Reformers’ refusal to grant Rome’s gospel a place alongside their own was an application of it, not an excess of zeal.

The opposite abuse must be named too, because this text has been used to justify separation from brethren over matters John was not discussing. The doctrine of Christ is the boundary here — not the millennial position, not the mode of church government, not every difference on which a faithful man may err. To wield 2 John against the confessionally orthodox is to make a rule for heretics do work against brothers, and it produces the sectarianism that has repeatedly fractured otherwise sound churches. Genesis 24 supplies the positive picture the word was made for: a servant asking God for good speed in a lawful errand, and receiving it before he had done speaking.
roots_summary: Hebrew qarah (H7136), to cause to meet or occur favourably; Greek chairo (G5463), to rejoice, used as a greeting; the KJV phrase God speed renders the ordinary Greek salutation.
roots_lines: Hebrew qarah (H7136) — to cause to occur, to bring about a meeting; send me good speed this day (Genesis 24:12).
Greek chairo (G5463) — to rejoice, and as a greeting hail; the word behind God speed in 2 John 1:10-11.
Greek koinoneo (G2841) — to share in, to be partaker of; the consequence John attaches to the greeting (2 John 1:11).
Anglo-Saxon sped — success, prosperity; the original English sense preserved in the Authorized Version.
Hebrew tsalach (H6743) — to prosper, to succeed; the standing Old Testament word for a prospered way.
usage: Send me good speed this day (Genesis 24:12) — a prayer for success in an errand, answered before he had finished speaking.
Neither bid him God speed (2 John 1:10) — the church’s blessing withheld from a denier of the incarnation.
He that biddeth him God speed is partaker of his evil deeds (2 John 1:11) — a blessing transfers a share.

etymology: From here and in: in this thing, in this respect. Webster 1828: in this. John uses it as a pointer, and where he points is the definition of love, the ground of assurance, and the glory of the Father.
biblical_def: John’s herein is one of the great pointing words of the New Testament. It appears where he means to fix the reader’s eye on a definition and not let it drift: Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins (1 John 4:10). The sentence defines love by an act, and by an act whose direction is from God to man; the negative clause — not that we loved God — is there to prevent the reader from starting anywhere else. Three verses later he uses it again for assurance, and the ground is startling: Herein is our love made perfect, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment: because as he is, so are we in this world (1 John 4:17). Our Lord uses the same construction for the Father’s glory and makes fruitfulness the evidence of discipleship: Herein is my Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit; so shall ye be my disciples (John 15:8). Paul uses it of settled practice under examination: herein do I exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men (Acts 24:16).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines HEREIN as in this — that is, in this thing, matter, respect, or particular.
webster_full: HEREIN, adv. — In this.
In this thing, matter, or particular; as, herein is our comfort.
Used to point emphatically at what immediately follows.
Compare HEREBY, by this; HEREOF, of this; HEREUPON, upon this.
From here and in; Anglo-Saxon her and in.
scriptures: 1 John 4:10
Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.
1 John 4:17
Herein is our love made perfect, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment: because as he is, so are we in this world.
John 15:8
Herein is my Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit; so shall ye be my disciples.
Acts 24:16
And herein do I exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men.
corruption_summary: 1 John 4:10 defines love by propitiation, and every account of the atonement that removes the appeasing of God’s wrath removes the very thing John points at when he says herein.
corruption_paragraphs: Herein is love — and the thing pointed at is a propitiation. The Greek word hilasmos means the turning away of wrath, and it is the word John chooses to define love with. This is the exact point at which much modern atonement theology departs. The moral-influence theory (Abelard, revived by liberal Protestantism) makes the cross a demonstration that moves us; the governmental theory makes it a display upholding God’s rule; more recent popular writing has gone further and called penal substitution unworthy of God. Each of these must first empty the word John uses. But Scripture says God set forth His Son as a propitiation through faith in His blood (Romans 3:25), and it says so in order to declare God righteous in justifying the ungodly. Remove the propitiation and the love has nothing to consist of, since it is defined here by no other content.

1 John 4:17 grounds boldness in the day of judgment on something outside the believer: as he is, so are we in this world. The assurance is not a measurement of the Christian’s progress but a statement of his standing in Christ — which is why the verse can speak of love made perfect and boldness in judgment in the same breath without contradiction. The Reformed doctrine of justification by imputed righteousness is what makes such a sentence sayable. If a believer’s acceptance rested on his sanctification, boldness in the day of judgment would be presumption; resting on Christ’s obedience reckoned to him, it is simple faith. John 15:8 then keeps the balance: much fruit is the evidence of discipleship, never its ground.
roots_summary: Greek en touto, in this — the phrase rendered herein; hilasmos (G2434), propitiation; parresia (G3954), boldness or freedom of speech.
roots_lines: Greek en touto — literally in this; John’s pointing phrase, rendered herein and hereby throughout his epistle.
Greek hilasmos (G2434) — propitiation, the turning away of wrath; the content of love in 1 John 4:10.
Greek parresia (G3954) — boldness, confidence, freedom of speech; boldness in the day of judgment (1 John 4:17).
Greek teleioo (G5048) — to bring to completeness; our love made perfect (1 John 4:17).
Greek askeo (G778) — to exercise oneself, to take pains; Paul’s word for his settled practice (Acts 24:16).
usage: Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us (1 John 4:10) — the negative clause prevents the reader starting anywhere else.
Herein is our love made perfect, that we may have boldness in the day of judgment (1 John 4:17) — the ground is outside the believer.
Herein is my Father glorified, that ye bear much fruit (John 15:8) — fruit is the evidence of discipleship, never its ground.

etymology: From Latin necessarius, unavoidable, indispensable, from necesse, needful. Webster 1828: that must be; that cannot be otherwise; indispensably requisite. Job uses it of food and then ranks the word of God above it.
biblical_def: Job’s protest of integrity contains a sentence that has been the food of the church ever since: Neither have I gone back from the commandment of his lips; I have esteemed the words of his mouth more than my necessary food (Job 23:12). Necessary here means what the body cannot do without — the daily ration — and Job says Scripture ranks above it. That is a considered order of goods, spoken by a man who at that moment had lost nearly everything else. The Jerusalem council uses the word of the minimum laid on Gentile believers: it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things (Acts 15:28) — and the striking feature is the restraint, since the council could have imposed the whole law and deliberately did not. Paul applies the word to the church’s weakest members, and reverses the world’s estimate: those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary (1 Corinthians 12:22). Not tolerated, not accommodated — necessary. And Titus is told to teach the profitable use of labour: let ours also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful (Titus 3:14).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines NECESSARY as that must be; that cannot be otherwise; indispensably requisite; unavoidable; and as a noun, things indispensable to a purpose.
webster_full: NECESSARY, a. — That must be; that cannot be otherwise; indispensably requisite.
Indispensable; requisite; essential; that cannot be otherwise without preventing the purpose intended.
Unavoidable; inevitable; as, a necessary consequence.
NECESSARY, n. — That which is indispensably requisite to a purpose; commonly used in the plural, necessaries.
Latin necessarius, from necesse, needful — that from which there is no yielding or retreat.
scriptures: Neither have I gone back from the commandment of his lips; I have esteemed the words of his mouth more than my necessary food.
Acts 15:28
For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things;
1 Corinthians 12:22
Nay, much more those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary:
Titus 3:14
And let ours also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful.
corruption_summary: Acts 15:28 shows a council refusing to bind consciences beyond what God requires, which is the standing rebuke to every addition made to Scripture as a term of communion.
corruption_paragraphs: The Jerusalem council had the authority and the occasion to impose the whole Mosaic economy on Gentile converts, and it declined. The phrase no greater burden than these necessary things is the New Testament’s own statement of Christian liberty, and the epistle to the Galatians is the same argument at length. This is the principle behind sola Scriptura as the Reformers meant it: Scripture alone binds the conscience absolutely, and whatever is added — whether Rome’s traditions and councils, or a local church’s unwritten rules made into tests of fellowship — is an unnecessary burden that no one has the right to lay. The 1689 Confession says it exactly: God alone is Lord of the conscience, and has left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men which are in anything contrary to His word, or beside it, in matters of faith or worship.

1 Corinthians 12:22 sets the church’s valuation of persons against every scale the world uses. Paul does not say the feebler members are to be included, tolerated, or made to feel welcome; he says they are necessary — the body cannot do its work without them. This is a stronger claim than the language of accommodation, and it should be preferred to it. Where a church measures its members by contribution, visibility, or usefulness to a programme, it has adopted an anthropology Paul rejects in this chapter. And Job 23:12 sets the corresponding valuation of things: a man may lose his property, his children and his health, and still hold that the words of God’s mouth outrank his daily bread.
roots_summary: Hebrew choq (H2706), an appointed portion or allotted ration; Greek epanagkes (G1876), necessary, indispensable; anagkaios (G316), necessary, needful.
roots_lines: Hebrew choq (H2706) — an appointed portion or allotted ration; the necessary food of Job 23:12.
Greek epanagkes (G1876) — of necessity, indispensable; the council’s word in Acts 15:28.
Greek anagkaios (G316) — necessary, needful; are necessary (1 Corinthians 12:22) and necessary uses (Titus 3:14).
Greek baros (G922) — a weight or burden; what the council refused to add (Acts 15:28).
Greek astheneo (G770) — to be weak or feeble; the members Paul calls necessary (1 Corinthians 12:22).
usage: I have esteemed the words of his mouth more than my necessary food (Job 23:12) — a considered order of goods, spoken by a man who had lost everything else.
No greater burden than these necessary things (Acts 15:28) — a council with the authority to bind, declining to.
Those members... which seem to be more feeble, are necessary (1 Corinthians 12:22) — not tolerated; necessary.

etymology: From Latin praeparatio, from prae (before) and parare (to make ready). Webster 1828: the act of preparing or fitting a thing for use; previous measures of readiness. Paul makes it a piece of armour, and Proverbs traces it back to God.
biblical_def: Among the pieces of the whole armour of God, the footwear is the one most often passed over: your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace (Ephesians 6:15). The soldier’s sandal is not a weapon; it is what lets him stand his ground and go where he is sent, and the readiness supplied is the gospel of peace — a man at peace with God can be sent anywhere. Proverbs traces even the inward act of preparing to its source: The preparations of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, is from the LORD (Proverbs 16:1). Not merely the outcome but the readying itself is God’s work, which is why the same chapter can command a man to commit his works unto the LORD and promise that his thoughts shall be established. The word also names a day. The Gospels mark the timing of the burial by it: when the even was come, because it was the preparation, that is, the day before the sabbath (Mark 15:42) — the day on which Israel got ready for rest, and on which the Lord of the sabbath was laid in a tomb. John the Baptist’s whole office was this word in a person: Prepare ye the way of the LORD (Isaiah 40:3).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PREPARATION as the act of preparing or fitting a thing for a particular use; previous measures of adaptation; the state of being prepared or in readiness.
webster_full: PREPARATION, n. — The act or operation of preparing or fitting a thing for a particular purpose or use.
Previous measures of adaptation; as, preparations for war.
The state of being prepared or in readiness; as, a man in preparation for the event.
That which is prepared; something made or compounded for a particular purpose.
Latin praeparatio, from prae, before, and paro, to make ready — the root of repair and apparatus.
scriptures: Ephesians 6:15
And your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace;
Proverbs 16:1
The preparations of the heart in man, and the answer of the tongue, is from the LORD.
Mark 15:42
And now when the even was come, because it was the preparation, that is, the day before the sabbath,
Isaiah 40:3
The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the LORD, make straight in the desert a highway for our God.
corruption_summary: Proverbs 16:1 assigns even the inward preparing of the heart to the LORD, which is precisely the point at which synergistic accounts of conversion must qualify the text.
corruption_paragraphs: The preparations of the heart in man... is from the LORD. If the readying of the heart is God’s, then the decisive movement in conversion is not the sinner’s. This is the doctrine of effectual calling: the Spirit does not merely make salvation available and wait, He renews the will and thereby makes the sinner willing, so that the man comes freely and comes certainly. Arminian and semi-Pelagian accounts must at this point make the preparation a cooperative act in which the final determination rests with the creature, and the text will not divide that way — it says the preparations are from the LORD, without remainder. Philippians 2:13 states the same thing positively: it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of His good pleasure. The believer’s effort is real, commanded, and strenuous; it is not the origin of itself.

Ephesians 6:15 deserves rescue from a common misreading that turns the shoes into a duty to evangelize. The genitive is better taken as the readiness that the gospel of peace supplies: a man who is at peace with God is thereby made able to stand. That order matters pastorally. Believers are regularly exhorted to be bold, ready, and immovable, as though these were qualities to be summoned; Paul roots them in an accomplished peace they already possess through justification (Romans 5:1). Mark 15:42 sets the darkest instance of the word in the calendar: on the day appointed for getting ready to rest, the body of the Lord of the sabbath was laid in a borrowed tomb, and the true rest was being prepared in a way none of them yet understood.
roots_summary: Greek hetoimasia (G2091), readiness, preparation; paraskeue (G3904), the preparation day before the sabbath; Hebrew maarak (H4633), an arrangement or ordering; kun (H3559), to establish or make ready.
roots_lines: Greek hetoimasia (G2091) — readiness, preparedness; the preparation of the gospel of peace (Ephesians 6:15).
Greek paraskeue (G3904) — the day of preparation, the eve of the sabbath (Mark 15:42).
Hebrew maarak (H4633) — an arrangement, an ordering of thought; the preparations of the heart (Proverbs 16:1).
Hebrew kun (H3559) — to set upright, to establish, to make ready; the standing verb behind a heart prepared toward God.
Hebrew panah (H6437) — to turn, to clear a way; Prepare ye the way of the LORD (Isaiah 40:3).
usage: Your feet shod with the preparation of the gospel of peace (Ephesians 6:15) — a man at peace with God can be sent anywhere.
The preparations of the heart in man... is from the LORD (Proverbs 16:1) — not merely the outcome but the readying.
Because it was the preparation, that is, the day before the sabbath (Mark 15:42) — the Lord of the sabbath laid in a tomb on the day of getting ready.

etymology: From Old French maintenir, from Latin manu tenere, to hold in the hand. Webster 1828: to hold or keep in any particular state; to support; to defend; to vindicate. Scripture uses it for two things: the cause of the afflicted, which God maintains, and good works, which the church must.
biblical_def: Twice in one short chapter Paul tells Titus that believers must maintain good works, and the repetition is deliberate: This is a faithful saying, and these things I will that thou affirm constantly, that they which have believed in God might be careful to maintain good works (Titus 3:8), and again, let ours also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful (Titus 3:14). The verb is not perform but maintain — to hold up, to keep going, to sustain as a settled occupation. And the placement is everything: it stands immediately after the strongest denial of works-righteousness in the epistle, that He saved us not by works of righteousness which we have done (Titus 3:5). God is said to maintain what men cannot: I know that the LORD will maintain the cause of the afflicted, and the right of the poor (Psalm 140:12). Solomon prays that He would do it for a praying nation: Then hear thou in heaven their prayer and their supplication, and maintain their cause (1 Kings 8:45). The word belongs to a defender who takes a case in hand and does not let it fall.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MAINTAIN as to hold, preserve or keep in any particular state or condition; to support; to sustain; to defend; to vindicate; to justify by argument.
webster_full: MAINTAIN, v.t. — To hold, preserve or keep in any particular state or condition; to support; to sustain.
To hold; to keep; not to lose or surrender; as, to maintain a place or post.
To continue; to keep up; not to suffer to cease; as, to maintain a conversation.
To support with food, clothing and other conveniences; as, to maintain a family.
To vindicate; to justify; to defend by argument; as, to maintain one’s cause. From Latin manu tenere, to hold in the hand.
scriptures: Titus 3:8

This is a faithful saying, and these things I will that thou affirm constantly, that they which have believed in God might be careful to maintain good works. These things are good and profitable unto men.
Titus 3:14
And let ours also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful.
Psalm 140:12
I know that the LORD will maintain the cause of the afflicted, and the right of the poor.
1 Kings 8:45
Then hear thou in heaven their prayer and their supplication, and maintain their cause.
corruption_summary: Titus 3 puts the strongest denial of works-righteousness three verses before the strongest charge to maintain good works, and both halves are routinely lost, each by a different party.
corruption_paragraphs: Titus 3:5 says plainly that He saved us not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy, and Titus 3:8 immediately charges believers to be careful to maintain good works. The Reformation held both without embarrassment, and the formula is old: we are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone. Rome’s error at Trent was to make works part of the ground of justification, which destroys the assurance the gospel gives; the antinomian error is to treat the denial in verse 5 as though it made the command in verse 8 optional, which destroys the evidence the gospel produces. James 2 and Titus 3 say the same thing from opposite directions. The 1689 Confession states the balance precisely: good works are the fruits and evidences of a true and lively faith, and by them believers manifest their thankfulness — not procure their pardon.

The second half of the verb is worth pressing. Paul does not say perform good works but maintain them, and the qualifier in verse 14 is for necessary uses — useful, ordinary, sustained provision for real needs, not conspicuous acts. That is a different vision of Christian usefulness from the one that measures a church by its programmes and campaigns. Psalm 140:12 supplies the ground under it: the LORD maintains the cause of the afflicted and the right of the poor, and the believer who maintains good works is doing in a small way what God does in a large one. The word belongs to defenders who take a case in hand and do not let it drop.
roots_summary: Greek proistemi (G4291), to stand before, to maintain or practise diligently; Hebrew asah din, to execute judgment; mishpat (H4941), judgment, the right of a cause.
roots_lines: Greek proistemi (G4291) — to stand before, to preside, and so to maintain or practise; careful to maintain good works (Titus 3:8, 3:14).
Hebrew din (H1777) — to plead a cause, to execute judgment; the LORD will maintain the cause of the afflicted (Psalm 140:12).
Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, justice, the right belonging to a cause (Psalm 140:12).
Hebrew asah (H6213) — to do or execute; used with mishpat for maintaining a people’s cause (1 Kings 8:45).
Greek akarpos (G175) — unfruitful, barren; the condition Titus 3:14 is written to prevent.
usage: Careful to maintain good works (Titus 3:8) — three verses after the strongest denial of works-righteousness in the epistle.
Maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful (Titus 3:14) — useful and sustained, not conspicuous.
The LORD will maintain the cause of the afflicted (Psalm 140:12) — a defender who takes a case in hand and does not let it fall.

etymology: From Latin directus, past participle of dirigere, to set straight, from dis- and regere, to rule or make straight. Webster 1828: to aim or point in a straight line toward a place or object; to order; to instruct. Scripture uses it of paths, prayers, and hearts — and denies the ability to man.
biblical_def: The best-known promise attached to this word comes with a condition that is often dropped: In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths (Proverbs 3:6). The preceding verse forbids leaning on one’s own understanding, so the directing is offered to a man who has stopped steering. Jeremiah states the negative behind it as a flat impossibility: O LORD, I know that the way of man is not in himself: it is not in man that walketh to direct his steps (Jeremiah 10:23) — not merely that a man ought not, but that he cannot. The word is used of prayer as a deliberate aiming: My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up (Psalm 5:3). David does not drift into prayer; he sets it, as an archer sets an arrow or a priest lays the wood in order. And Paul prays for the same divine steering over ordinary travel plans: Now God himself and our Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ, direct our way unto you (1 Thessalonians 3:11), a request from a man whose itinerary had already been redirected more than once.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines DIRECT as to aim or point in a straight line toward a place or object; to point, to show the right road or course; to order, instruct, or command.
webster_full: DIRECT, v.t. — To aim or point in a straight line toward a place or object; as, to direct an arrow.
To point out to another, as a course; to show the right road or course.
To order; to instruct; to command; to give authoritative direction to.
To regulate; to guide or lead; to govern; as, to direct the affairs of a nation.
DIRECT, a. — Straight; right; not crooked or oblique. Latin directus, from dirigo, to make straight.
scriptures: Proverbs 3:6
In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.
Jeremiah 10:23
O LORD, I know that the way of man is not in himself: it is not in man that walketh to direct his steps.
Psalm 5:3
My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up.
1 Thessalonians 3:11
Now God himself and our Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ, direct our way unto you.
corruption_summary: Proverbs 3:6 has become a promise of subjective guidance detached from its condition and from the written word, producing Christians who look for inward impressions where God has given commandments.
corruption_paragraphs: The verse is regularly quoted as an assurance that God will supply an inward sense of which choice to make. That is not what it says. The condition is acknowledging Him in all thy ways, set against leaning on one’s own understanding, and the directing promised is the ordering of a life by One who is trusted — not a stream of impressions about jobs and houses. The practical damage of the popular reading is considerable: believers become anxious about discerning a hidden individual will while neglecting the revealed will that fills the Scriptures, and decisions get made on the strength of feelings that no one can test. The Reformed and Puritan counsel is steadier — obey what God has plainly commanded, use sanctified wisdom and counsel in what He has left free, pray as David did, and trust providence to order the outcome.

Jeremiah 10:23 is one of the strongest statements of creaturely dependence in the Old Testament and it is not addressed to the wicked in particular: it is not in man that walketh to direct his steps. This is not a denial that men make real choices; the same Scriptures hold men fully responsible for theirs. It is a denial of autonomy — the notion that a man is the origin and governor of his own course. Proverbs 16:9 pairs the two halves exactly: a man’s heart deviseth his way, but the LORD directeth his steps. The devising is genuinely his; the directing is genuinely God’s. Every doctrine of providence that dissolves either clause — fatalism on one side, autonomy on the other — has taken half a verse.
roots_summary: Hebrew yashar (H3474), to make straight or smooth; kun (H3559), to establish or make firm; arak (H6186), to set in order or arrange; Greek kateuthuno (G2720), to make straight, to direct.
roots_lines: Hebrew yashar (H3474) — to make straight or level; he shall direct thy paths (Proverbs 3:6).
Hebrew kun (H3559) — to establish, to make firm; the LORD directeth his steps (Proverbs 16:9).
Hebrew arak (H6186) — to arrange or set in order, as wood on an altar; will I direct my prayer unto thee (Psalm 5:3).
Greek kateuthuno (G2720) — to make straight, to guide; direct our way unto you (1 Thessalonians 3:11).
Hebrew tsaad (H6806) — a step or pace; the unit of the way a man cannot direct (Jeremiah 10:23).
usage: In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths (Proverbs 3:6) — offered to a man who has stopped steering.
It is not in man that walketh to direct his steps (Jeremiah 10:23) — not merely that he ought not, but that he cannot.
In the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee (Psalm 5:3) — David sets his prayer as an archer sets an arrow.

etymology: From Old French norir, from Latin nutrire, to suckle, to feed, to bring up. Webster 1828: fed; supported; brought up; nurtured. The word carries the sense of long feeding rather than a single meal, which is exactly why Paul chooses it for a minister’s formation.
biblical_def: Paul’s picture of a faithful minister is not a man with a gift but a man who has been fed: thou shalt be a good minister of Jesus Christ, nourished up in the words of faith and of good doctrine, whereunto thou hast attained (1 Timothy 4:6). The tense and the compound both point backward — Timothy is what years of doctrine have made him, and the immediately preceding clause tells him how to keep it up: by putting the brethren in remembrance of these things. A man is nourished by the doctrine he feeds to others. Luke uses the same word for an infancy that shaped a deliverer: Moses, when he was cast out, Pharaoh's daughter took him up, and nourished him for her own son (Acts 7:21). James turns it into an indictment, and the image is agricultural and terrible: Ye have lived in pleasure on the earth, and been wanton; ye have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter (James 5:5) — men fattening themselves on the very day the beasts are killed. The word can even describe a dependency between nations: Tyre and Sidon sought peace with Herod because their country was nourished by the king's country (Acts 12:20).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines NOURISH as to feed and cause to grow; to supply a living being with matter which increases its bulk or supplies the waste of its organs; to support; to maintain; to educate; hence NOURISHED, fed, supported, brought up.
webster_full: NOURISH, v.t. — To feed and cause to grow; to supply a living being with matter which increases its bulk or supplies the waste of its organs.
To support; to maintain by feeding; as, to nourish a family.
To educate; to instruct; to bring up; to promote growth in attainments.
To cherish; to encourage; to foster; as, to nourish a hope, or a rebellion.
NOURISHED, pp. — Fed; supplied with nutriment; caused to grow; educated. Latin nutrio, to feed.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 4:6
If thou put the brethren in remembrance of these things, thou shalt be a good minister of Jesus Christ, nourished up in the words of faith and of good doctrine, whereunto thou hast attained.
Acts 7:21
And when he was cast out, Pharaoh's daughter took him up, and nourished him for her own son.
James 5:5
Ye have lived in pleasure on the earth, and been wanton; ye have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter.
Acts 12:20

And Herod was highly displeased with them of Tyre and Sidon: but they came with one accord to him, and, having made Blastus the king's chamberlain their friend, desired peace; because their country was nourished by the king's country.
corruption_summary: 1 Timothy 4:6 makes doctrine the minister’s food rather than his equipment, which the modern pastorate has largely inverted by treating theology as a seminary stage to be passed.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul does not tell Timothy to use good doctrine; he says a good minister is nourished up in it, and the metaphor is nutrition, not tooling. Doctrine is what a man is made of, laid down over years, and the loss of that picture is the root of much that ails the modern pastorate. Where theology is treated as a credential obtained early and thereafter drawn upon, a ministry runs on stored reserves and eventually on technique. Where it is treated as daily food, it keeps building the man. Notice too the order of the verse: Timothy is nourished by putting the brethren in remembrance — the feeding of the flock is part of how the shepherd is fed. The Puritan practice of preaching one’s way through Scripture, and the confessional practice of catechizing, both assume this and are worth recovering for this reason alone.

James 5:5 supplies the counter-image and it is the sharper of the two: ye have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter. The rich men James addresses are feeding themselves well, and the figure is livestock fattened on the very morning the knife is out. Scripture’s objection is not to wealth as such — Abraham and Job were rich, and Scripture does not apologize for it — but to a heart nourished by pleasure and indifferent to the judgment standing at the door (James 5:9). It is worth naming the prosperity teaching here in the same breath: a gospel that promises exactly the fattening James condemns, and calls the fattening evidence of God’s favour, has read this chapter backwards.
roots_summary: Greek entrepho (G1789), to nourish up in, to train; anatrepho (G397), to bring up, to rear; trepho (G5142), to feed or fatten.
roots_lines: Greek entrepho (G1789) — to nourish up in, to train within something; nourished up in the words of faith (1 Timothy 4:6).
Greek anatrepho (G397) — to bring up, to rear from infancy; used of Moses in Pharaoh’s house (Acts 7:21).
Greek trepho (G5142) — to feed, and of animals to fatten; ye have nourished your hearts (James 5:5).
Greek sphage (G4967) — slaughter; the day on which James’s rich men are fattening (James 5:5).
Greek didaskalia (G1319) — teaching, doctrine; the substance Timothy is nourished in (1 Timothy 4:6).
usage: Nourished up in the words of faith and of good doctrine (1 Timothy 4:6) — doctrine as food, not as equipment.
Nourished him for her own son (Acts 7:21) — providence rearing a deliverer in the house of the oppressor.
Ye have nourished your hearts, as in a day of slaughter (James 5:5) — livestock fattened on the morning the knife is out.

etymology: From work and man: one who labours, particularly with skill in a trade. Webster 1828: any man employed in labour, whether in husbandry or manufactures; a skilful artificer. Paul makes it the figure for a minister handling Scripture, and Isaiah makes it the figure for a man manufacturing a god.
biblical_def: Paul’s charge to Timothy uses a tradesman’s language throughout: Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth (2 Timothy 2:15). Every clause is deliberate. The approval sought is God’s, not the congregation’s; the shame in view is the shame of shoddy work; and rightly dividing renders a word meaning to cut straight, as a mason squares a stone or a farmer drives a straight furrow. Handling Scripture is a craft with a standard, and a man can be sincere and still botch it. Our Lord establishes the labourer’s right to support: the workman is worthy of his meat (Matthew 10:10), a principle Paul repeats in 1 Timothy 5:18 and applies to elders. The word turns dark in the prophets, where the workman’s skill is spent on an idol: The workman melteth a graven image, and the goldsmith spreadeth it over with gold (Isaiah 40:19). Hosea draws the conclusion with a logic no idolater can answer: For from Israel was it also: the workman made it; therefore it is not God: but the calf of Samaria shall be broken in pieces (Hosea 8:6).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines WORKMAN as any man employed in labour, whether in husbandry or manufactures; and more particularly a skilful artificer or laborer, one who is skilled in any trade or manual occupation.
webster_full: WORKMAN, n. — Any man employed in labor, whether in husbandry or manufactures.
More generally, a skilful artificer or laborer; one skilled in any manual occupation.
WORKMANSHIP, n. — The skill of a workman; the execution or manner of making anything.
That which is effected, made or produced; the thing wrought.
From work, Anglo-Saxon weorc, and man.
scriptures: 2 Timothy 2:15
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth.
Matthew 10:10
Nor scrip for your journey, neither two coats, neither shoes, nor yet staves: for the workman is worthy of his meat.
Isaiah 40:19
The workman melteth a graven image, and the goldsmith spreadeth it over with gold, and casteth silver chains.
Hosea 8:6
For from Israel was it also: the workman made it; therefore it is not God: but the calf of Samaria shall be broken in pieces.
corruption_summary: 2 Timothy 2:15 assumes there is a right and a wrong way to cut the text, which is exactly what the reader-response habit of asking what a passage means to me denies.
corruption_paragraphs: Rightly dividing translates orthotomeo, to cut straight — a word from trades where a crooked cut ruins the material. The charge presupposes that a passage has a meaning the workman can either hit or miss, and that missing it is culpable. This is the point at which the now-common practice of asking a group what a verse means to them fails, not because personal application is wrong but because it substitutes for interpretation. Scripture has an author and therefore a determinate sense; the reader’s task is to find it, and the Reformers’ insistence on the literal or plain sense, read in context and with Scripture interpreting Scripture, is the discipline that makes finding it possible. The 1689 Confession adds the rule that the infallible interpreter of Scripture is Scripture itself, which is a workman’s rule as much as a theologian’s.

Isaiah and Hosea show what a workman’s skill produces when it is turned on God. Hosea’s argument is a single unanswerable inference: the workman made it; therefore it is not God. Anything a craftsman can produce is by definition beneath him, and Isaiah 40 spends the whole chapter pressing the absurdity, moving from the God who holds the seas in His palm to the man carefully choosing a tree that will not rot. The second commandment forbids images of God for this reason, and the prohibition is not aesthetic but logical: any representation a workman can make will misrepresent. The dictionary’s regulative principle of worship is the same argument applied to practice — what God has not commanded in worship is workmanship, however skilled.
roots_summary: Greek ergates (G2040), a workman or labourer; orthotomeo (G3718), to cut straight; Hebrew charash (H2796), an engraver or craftsman; maaseh (H4639), a work or thing made.
roots_lines: Greek ergates (G2040) — a workman, a labourer; a workman that needeth not to be ashamed (2 Timothy 2:15) and the workman is worthy of his meat (Matthew 10:10).
Greek orthotomeo (G3718) — to cut straight, as a road or a furrow; rightly dividing the word of truth (2 Timothy 2:15).
Hebrew charash (H2796) — a craftsman, engraver, or smith; the workman melteth a graven image (Isaiah 40:19).
Greek dokimos (G1384) — approved after testing; the standing the workman seeks from God (2 Timothy 2:15).
Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a carved or graven image, the workman’s product forbidden by the second commandment.
usage: A workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth (2 Timothy 2:15) — handling Scripture is a craft with a standard.
The workman is worthy of his meat (Matthew 10:10) — the labourer’s right to support, applied by Paul to elders.
The workman made it; therefore it is not God (Hosea 8:6) — a single unanswerable inference against every idol.
